genus, Homo, stretches back close to 3
million years. But the controlled,
regular use of fire, not occasional
opportunistic use of natural wildfires,
but the actual deliberate maintenance
and use of fire as a routine technology,
appears to have become widespread and
consistent somewhere in the range of
400,000 to 1 million years ago, with
some evidence suggesting earlier
sporadic use, but genuine debate over
how routine and widespread that early
use actually was.
This means that for an enormous stretch
of hominin evolutionary history,
stretching back millions of years before
any consistent fire use, our ancestors
were eating an entirely raw diet and
were doing so not as some kind of
survivalist novelty, but as the only
available option, generation after
generation after generation. Let us
begin with meat because meat consumption
is one of the most heavily discussed and
most consequential dietary shifts in the
entire hominin evolutionary record and
it happened long before fire entered the
picture.
The archaeological evidence for meat
consumption among early hominins
predates controlled fire use by an
enormous margin. Cut marks on animal
bones, produced by stone tools used to
butcher carcasses, appear in the
archaeological record at sites dating
back at least 2.5 million years and some
evidence pushes this date even earlier.
This means hominins were eating meat,
raw meat by definition, since fire was
not yet in routine use, for well over a
million years before they had any way to
cook it.
What did raw meat consumption actually
involve, practically speaking? The
honest answer is that it involved
considerably more chewing than modern
humans are accustomed to, a genuine and
persistent risk of parasitic and
bacterial infection, and a digestive
system specifically adapted to handle
these challenges in ways that modern
human digestive systems, shaped by
hundreds of thousands of years of cooked
food consumption, have partially lost.
Raw meat is mechanically tough. Muscle
fibers, connective tissue, and cartilage
in uncooked meat require significantly
more chewing force and significantly
more time to break down into swallowable
portions compared to cooked meat, where
heat has already begun the process of
breaking down collagen and softening
muscle fiber structure.
This is part of why early hominin skulls
show such robust jaw musculature and
such large molars relative to modern
humans. The mechanical demands of
processing raw, tough food required
genuinely powerful chewing apparatus
that later softened anatomically as
cooking gradually reduced these
mechanical demands.
The bacterial and parasitic risk
associated with raw meat consumption was
genuinely significant. Modern food
safety guidelines exist precisely
because raw and undercooked meat carries
meaningful risk of pathogens, including
various Salmonella strains, E. coli,
Listeria, and numerous parasitic
organisms, all of which are
substantially reduced or eliminated by
adequate cooking temperatures.
Early hominins eating raw meat were
exposed to all of these risks without
any of the modern interventions that
mitigate these dangers today.
This raises an obvious and genuinely
interesting question. How did early
hominins survive this level of exposure
to food-borne pathogens for millions of
years? The answer appears to involve
hominin gut physiology, including
stomach acidity levels, being somewhat
more aggressive in its pathogen-killing
capacity than is strictly necessary for
a cooked food diet, providing a buffer
against the elevated pathogen load of
raw food consumption.
Second, and this deserves real emphasis,
hominins [snorts]
almost certainly suffered genuinely
significant rates of illness and
mortality directly attributable to raw
food consumption, and simply survived
this burden as one of many mortality
risks in an environment already
characterized by extraordinarily high
background mortality from numerous other
sources.
Beyond raw meat, early hominins almost
certainly consumed organ meats with
particular enthusiasm.
Organ meats, liver, kidney, brain,
marrow, are considerably softer and more
mechanically tractable than muscle
tissue, requiring far less chewing
effort to consume raw, while
simultaneously offering extremely high
concentrations of specific nutrients.
Bone marrow deserves particular
attention because the archaeological
evidence for marrow extraction among
early hominins is genuinely extensive.
Many cut marks and percussion marks
found on ancient animal bones are
specifically consistent with deliberate
bone breaking intended to access the
marrow cavity.
Marrow is essentially pure fat,
calorically dense, and would have
represented an extremely efficient
source of concentrated calories for a
species working with a raw, unprocessed
food supply.
There is also a genuinely interesting
strategic dimension to early hominin
meat acquisition because a substantial
body of evidence suggests early
hominins, particularly in the earlier
phases of the genus Homo, may have
relied significantly on scavenging.
Accessing carcasses that had already
been killed by other predators.
This scavenging strategy has specific
implications for what was actually being
eaten since scavenged carcasses range
from relatively fresh to genuinely well
into the process of decomposition.
Many scavenging species, including
hyenas and vultures, regularly consume
meat well into advanced stages of
decomposition without apparent harm, and
the practical reality of a
scavenging-dependent diet almost
certainly meant that at least some
portion of the meat being consumed was
considerably less fresh than what any
modern person would willingly eat. Now,
let us turn to the plant side of the
pre-fire diet because plant foods almost
certainly represented the bulk of
caloric intake for most hominin
populations across most of this
evolutionary period. The specific
challenge with raw plant consumption
involves the digestibility of starch.
Many of the most calorically dense plant
foods available to early hominins,
tubers, roots, and various underground
storage organs, contain starch in a form
that is significantly more difficult for
the human digestive system to break down
when raw compared to when cooked.
Raw starch exists in a crystalline
structure that human digestive enzymes
have considerable difficulty accessing
efficiently.
Cooking disrupts this crystalline
structure through gelatinization, in
which heat and moisture cause starch
granules to swell and rupture, exposing
far more surface area to digestive
enzymes.
Studies comparing the caloric yield of
raw versus cooked starchy foods have
found substantial differences, with a
meaningful percentage of raw starch
passing through the human digestive
system essentially undigested. This
raises an interesting evolutionary
puzzle that researchers, including
Richard Wrangham, have spent
considerable effort addressing. If raw
starchy tubers provided meaningfully
reduced caloric value, how did early
hominins extract sufficient calories
from plant sources before fire made this
problem easier?
Several mechanisms appear to have been
involved. First, mechanical processing
short of actual cooking does provide
some genuine benefit. Pounding, mashing,
and thorough chewing increases surface
area exposed to digestive enzymes.
Second, fermentation, whether managed or
simply an inevitable consequence of
plant foods left in warm conditions,
provides another mechanism for improving
digestibility without fire.
Third, and perhaps most important, early
hominins almost certainly relied more
heavily on plant foods that did not
present the same raw starch
digestibility problem. Fruits, when
ripe, contain sugars in forms directly
absorbable without enzymatic breakdown,
and nuts and seeds contain fats and
proteins that do not face the same
digestibility gap. This suggests the
pre-fire hominin diet likely emphasized
fruits, nuts, seeds, and leafy plant
material more heavily relative to
starchy tubers and roots than the
post-fire diet eventually did,
with tubers and roots becoming
dramatically more nutritionally valuable
specifically after cooking became
routine and reliable. There is also the
matter of insects, which deserves more
in popular discussions of ancient
hominin diet than it typically receives.
Insects represented an extremely
accessible, reliable, and nutritionally
dense food source that required no
cooking to be both palatable and
nutritionally valuable.
Comparative studies of contemporary
great apes, particularly chimpanzees,
document extensive and sophisticated
insect foraging behavior, including the
use of tools to extract termites and
ants from their nests. Termites, ants,
grubs, and various beetle larvae would
have represented a reliable, year-round,
easily accessible source of fat and
protein that required no fire and
relatively modest foraging effort
relative to the caloric return. Honey
deserves specific mention as well
because it represents one of the most
calorically dense and most immediately
accessible food sources available,
requiring absolutely no processing to be
consumed and digested with full
efficiency.
The challenge with honey was not
digestibility but acquisition, given
that wild honey is typically defended by
bees in ways that make extraction
genuinely risky. There is a specific
anatomical line of evidence worth
exploring in more depth because the
human digestive tract itself preserves a
kind of physical record of this entire
dietary transition. The human
gastrointestinal tract is, relative to
body size, notably smaller than that of
our closest living primate relatives,
particularly when comparing the relative
size of the colon. This reduction in
human gut size is widely interpreted as
a direct consequence of cooking on the
logic that a smaller gut became
metabolically viable once cooking began
reliably pre-processing food in ways
that reduce the digestive workload
previously handled by gut tissue itself.
This connects directly to one of the
more compelling arguments in the broader
scientific literature about human brain
evolution, sometimes referred to as the
expensive tissue hypothesis, developed
by researchers including Leslie Aiello
and Peter Wheeler. The core argument
holds that the human brain's unusually
large size was made metabolically
possible specifically because the human
gut shrank in compensation, freeing up
the substantial metabolic budget that a
larger ape-like gut would otherwise have
consumed. If this argument holds, a
hominin population still relying on a
larger, more ape-like gut to extract
sufficient energy from a raw diet would
have been operating under genuinely
tighter metabolic constraints on brain
size than later hominins who had access
to cooking. Let us also consider dental
evidence, because microwear analysis,
the study of microscopic scratches and
pits on tooth enamel, has been applied
extensively to early hominin fossil
teeth, and the results consistently
support a diet involving substantial
mechanical processing demands consistent
with raw, tough, fibrous food. Not all
early hominins show identical wear
patterns, suggesting genuine dietary
specialization even within the broader
category of pre-fire raw diet
consumption.
Some early hominin species, particularly
within the genus Paranthropus, show
dental and jaw morphology suggesting
specialization toward extremely tough,
fibrous plant material requiring
exceptional mechanical processing
capacity.
Other early Homo species show somewhat
less extreme dental specialization,
consistent with a more varied and more
behaviorally flexible diet. This dietary
divergence across different hominin
lineages is itself fascinating, because
it suggests the pre-fire diet was never
a single, uniform strategy practiced
identically across every hominin
population. Some specialized toward
extreme mechanical processing capacity
for tough plant material.
Others, including the lineage that
eventually led to modern humans, appear
to have pursued a more flexible,
behaviorally adaptable strategy relying
more heavily on behavioral flexibility,
tool use, and strategic food choice than
on extreme anatomical specialization.
There is also a comparative dimension
worth exploring involving contemporary
individuals who have, for various
reasons, maintained substantially raw
diets in the modern era.
Studies of contemporary individuals
following strict raw food diets have
found measurable differences compared to
individuals eating a typical cooked
diet, including lower body mass index
and, in women specifically, increased
rates of amenorrhea, generally
attributed to insufficient caloric
intake given the documented reduction in
caloric extraction efficiency from raw
food.
This comparative modern evidence
reinforces that the pre-fire hominin
diet was not some kind of secretly
superior, naturally optimized strategy
that modern humans have unfortunately
abandoned.
It was a genuinely more difficult, more
costly, more risk-laden dietary strategy
that hominins persisted with for
millions of years because it was the
only option available before fire
provided a dramatically better
alternative. There is one more strand
worth pulling concerning seasonal and
geographic variation in the pre-fire
diet.
Hominin populations spreading across
Africa and eventually other continents
would have encountered enormously varied
environments, each presenting a
genuinely different mix of available raw
food resources. In tropical forest
environments, fruit and insect
availability would have been relatively
consistent across much of the year.
Savannah environments would have
presented considerably more dramatic
seasonal variation with dry season
scarcity making meat and underground
storage organs proportionally more
important precisely because they
remained available even when more easily
digestible plant resources had become
scarce. This seasonal and geographic
variation suggests the pre-fire diet
required hominin populations to shift
their relative reliance on different
food categories depending on local
conditions, demanding accumulated
environmental knowledge and strategic
decision-making capacity.
Some researchers have argued these
cognitive demands may themselves have
contributed to selective pressure
favoring increased cognitive capacity in
early hominin populations independent of
and prior to the additional cognitive
benefits that cooking would eventually
provide.
The hominin lineage that eventually
produced modern humans did not survive
by having any single overwhelming
anatomical advantage over other species.
Early hominins were not particularly
fast, particularly strong, or
particularly well defended against
predators. What they appear to have had
consistently was behavioral flexibility,
the capacity to strategically assess
available resources, use simple tools to
overcome processing challenges, shift
dietary strategy in response to
variation, and tolerate genuine costs
and risks that a less behaviorally
sophisticated species might not have
managed. The pre-fire diet, in this
light, was not simply a difficult
chapter that hominins endured before the
real story began.
It was itself an essential part of that
story, a multi-million-year proving
ground during which the behavioral and
cognitive flexibility that would
eventually define our entire species was
being tested and selected for. One raw
meal, one foraged tuber, one scavenged
carcass, and one handful of insects at a
time. There is a genuinely underexplored
dimension of this entire story worth
bringing in now, and it concerns water,
which sounds like an odd thing to dwell
on in a discussion of food, but which
connects directly and importantly to the
broader question of what pre-fire
hominin survival actually required, and
how tightly interconnected the various
survival challenges of this period
genuinely were. Fire, once it became
available, did not just transform food.
It also transformed water safety in ways
that are easy to overlook when thinking
specifically about diet, but that matter
enormously when reconstructing the full
survival context that pre-fire hominins
were operating within.
Boiling water kills the vast majority of
waterborne pathogens, including various
bacteria, protozoa, and parasites that
would otherwise pose genuine and ongoing
health risks to anyone drinking from
natural water sources.
Before fire, hominins drinking from
rivers, streams, ponds, and other
natural water sources had no equivalent
mechanism for reducing this pathogen
load, meaning that waterborne illness,
alongside the foodborne illness risks
already discussed at length, would have
represented a persistent and unavoidable
background health risk throughout this
entire period. This matters for our
broader picture because it suggests the
pre-fire hominin health burden was not
limited to food-specific risks alone. It
extended across essentially every
category of ingested substance, food,
and water alike, creating a genuinely
demanding overall disease environment
that early hominin populations had to
survive within.
Generation after generation, using
nothing but whatever innate
physiological resilience and behavioral
risk avoidance strategies they had
managed to develop. Choosing water
sources carefully, based on accumulated
experiential knowledge about which
sources tended to produce illness and
which did not, would have represented
another genuine cognitive and behavioral
demand layered on top of everything else
we have already discussed regarding food
acquisition and processing strategy. Let
us also spend a moment considering the
specific question of food storage and
preservation in the pre-fire period
because this is another dimension of
pre-fire survival that connects directly
to dietary strategy, and that deserves
more careful attention than it typically
receives in popular discussions focused
primarily on what specific foods were
eaten, rather than how those foods were
managed over time.
Without fire, and specifically without
the smoking and drying techniques that
fire eventually made possible, pre-fire
hominins had genuinely limited options
for preserving food beyond its natural
shelf life. Meat from a large kill or
scavenged carcass would have begun
decomposing relatively quickly,
particularly in warm climates, creating
real pressure to consume available meat
resources rapidly, rather than
attempting to preserve them for later
use.
This time pressure almost certainly
shaped hominin social behavior around
large food acquisitions in genuinely
significant ways, likely contributing to
the kind of immediate, group-wide meat
sharing that has been extensively
documented in studies of contemporary
hunter-gatherer societies, and that
appears, based on various lines of
archaeological evidence, to have deep
roots extending back into this much
earlier pre-fire period as well. The
logic here is fairly direct. If a large
kill cannot be effectively preserved and
will simply rot if not consumed
promptly, the optimal strategy becomes
rapid, wide distribution and consumption
of the available meat across as many
individuals as possible, both to avoid
waste and to build the kind of
reciprocal social relationships and
obligations that would prove valuable
when the sharing roles eventually
reversed, with a different individual or
family group becoming the temporary
holder of a large kill on some future
occasion.
This kind of reciprocal meat sharing
behavior, well documented in modern
hunter-gatherer ethnography, may have
origins that predate fire entirely,
driven initially by the simple
preservation problem that an undried,
unsmoked piece of meat presents in a
warm climate without refrigeration or
any other preservation technology.
Plant foods presented somewhat different
storage challenges depending on the
specific food category involved. Nuts
and seeds, with their naturally low
moisture content and protective shells
or husks, would have been considerably
easier to store for extended periods
without active preservation technology
compared to meat, fruit, or tubers, all
of which have higher moisture content
and correspondingly faster spoilage
timelines under most environmental
conditions. This differential
storability may have given nuts and
seeds a particular strategic value in
the pre-fire hominin diet beyond their
straightforward nutritional content,
functioning as a more reliable buffer
food resource that could be gathered
during periods of abundance and consumed
gradually over period in a way that more
perishable food categories simply could
not support. Tubers and roots,
interestingly, occupy an intermediate
position in the storage discussion
because many tuber species have evolved
their own natural storage capacity as
underground plant organs specifically
adapted to survive dormant periods,
meaning some tuber varieties can remain
viable and edible in the ground for
extended periods without requiring any
active preservation effort from hominin
foragers at all. This natural storage
capacity, combined with the simple
strategy of leaving tubers in the ground
until needed rather than harvesting them
all at once, would have provided early
hominins with a genuinely useful natural
food bank accessible across an extended
period without requiring any of the
active preservation technology that fire
would eventually provide for other food
categories. There is also a genuinely
interesting comparative angle worth
bringing into this discussion involving
contemporary chimpanzee dietary behavior
because chimpanzees represent our
closest living relatives and offer at
least some imperfect but genuinely
informative window into what a
sophisticated raw food primate diet can
actually look like in practice, observed
directly by researchers in real time
rather than reconstructed indirectly
from fossil and archaeological evidence
alone.
Extensive long-term field studies of
wild chimpanzee populations conducted
across multiple research sites in Africa
over several decades have documented an
extraordinarily varied diet
incorporating well over 100 distinct
plant species at some study sites
supplemented by insects, by
opportunistic meat consumption through
both scavenging and active hunting of
smaller animals, and by careful seasonal
tracking of which specific food
resources are available and worth
pursuing at any given point in the year.
This level of dietary sophistication and
behavioral flexibility documented
directly in a living observable primate
species provides genuinely strong
supporting evidence for the broader
argument we have been building
throughout this discussion. That
successfully managing a raw, unprocessed
diet across variable environmental
conditions requires and reflects genuine
behavioral and cognitive sophistication,
not simple passive consumption of
whatever happens to be available.
Chimpanzee hunting behavior specifically
deserves additional attention here
because it directly illuminates
questions about early hominin meat
acquisition that the archaeological
record alone cannot fully resolve.
Researchers have documented chimpanzees
engaging in coordinated group hunting of
smaller primates, including colobus
monkeys, using strategies that involve
role differentiation among hunting party
members,
and that produce meat sharing patterns
among successful hunters and other group
members that bear genuine resemblance to
patterns documented in human
hunter-gatherer societies. If
chimpanzees without any access to fire
or sophisticated tool technology beyond
simple sticks and stones are capable of
this level of coordinated hunting
behavior and structured meat
distribution, it provides reasonable
grounds for inferring that early
hominins, sharing a relatively recent
common ancestor with chimpanzees and
possessing at least comparable and
likely somewhat greater cognitive and
behavioral sophistication, were capable
of broadly similar or more advanced raw
meat acquisition strategies well before
fire entered the picture.
This comparative evidence also helps
address a specific question that
sometimes gets raised in discussions of
pre-fire hominin diet, whether early
hominins were primarily passive
scavengers, opportunistically consuming
whatever carrion happened to be
available, or active and capable hunters
in their own right, even without fire as
a technological aid. The honest answer,
based on the combined weight of
archaeological cut mark evidence,
comparative primate behavioral evidence,
and anatomical evidence related to
hominin physical capabilities,
suggests both strategies were almost
certainly employed.
Likely with the specific balance between
scavenging and active hunting shifting
across different hominin species,
different time periods, and different
specific environmental and ecological
circumstances, rather than either
strategy operating as the single
exclusive approach throughout this
entire extended pre-fire period.
Bringing this expanded discussion to a
close, what emerges is an even richer
and more textured picture of the
pre-fire dietary world than we had
already established.
It was a world defined not just by what
specific foods were available, and how
they were processed and consumed, but by
an entire interconnected web of survival
challenges, including water safety, food
preservation and storage strategy, and
the behavioral coordination required to
successfully acquire and distribute
resources like large game meat that
could not be preserved for extended
periods without the preservation
technology that fire would eventually
provide.
Every one of these challenges demanded
genuine behavioral sophistication and
accumulated environmental knowledge,
reinforcing the broader theme that has
run throughout this entire discussion.
The millions of years hominins spent
eating without fire were not simply a
deprived prelude to the real story of
human dietary development.
They were themselves a genuinely
demanding, genuinely sophisticated
chapter of that story, during which the
behavioral flexibility, strategic
thinking, and accumulated practical
knowledge that would eventually define
our species were being actively forged,
tested, and refined against the genuine
and unforgiving constraints that an
entirely raw food world imposed."}]

time anyone ever saw fire. Lightning has
been setting things ablaze for hundreds
of millions of years, and animals have
been fleeing it for just as long, but
the first time a hominin looked at fire
and had a thought that no animal before
them had ever had. Not run, not hide,
not the deep, ancient, wired-in command
to get away from the burning thing.
Something closer to, "Wait." We do not
know when that moment happened. We do
not know who it was, what species they
were, or what exactly was going through
their head when they stayed instead of
fled. What we do know is that at some
point in the deep prehistory of our
lineage, possibly as far back as 1.5 to
2 million years ago, some ancestor of
ours began a relationship with fire that
would end up being the most
consequential relationship in the
history of life on this planet. Not a
metaphor. Literally the most
consequential, more than photosynthesis
unlocking solar energy for complex life,
more than the Cambrian explosion of
animal body plans. Fire, in the hands of
a thinking primate, changed everything.
It changed what we ate, what we looked
like, how our brains developed, where we
could live, when we were awake, how we
related to each other, and ultimately
what kind of civilization we were
capable of building. The entire human
story after fire is different from
anything that came before it in ways
that most people have not fully reckoned
with. Let us start with the most
immediate and most dramatic consequence,
cooking. Before cooking, early hominins
ate raw food. This seems obvious, but
its implications are not. Raw food,
tubers, roots, meat, fruits, seeds, is
genuinely difficult to process. Raw meat
requires enormous chewing effort and is
harder to digest than cooked meat. Raw
plant starches are largely indigestible
without cooking because heat breaks down
the cell walls and converts resistant
starches into forms that the human gut
can actually absorb. Raw food also
carries a significant pathogen load. The
parasites, bacteria, and viruses that
live in uncooked meat and unwashed plant
material cause illness and death at
rates that cooked food dramatically
reduces. From a biological standpoint,
cooking is not just food preparation. It
is an external digestive process that
the body no longer has to perform
entirely on its own. Richard Wrangham, a
Harvard primatologist, has developed
what he calls the cooking hypothesis.
The argument that cooking was not just a
useful addition to the hominin toolkit,
but the primary driver of the anatomical
changes that distinguish Homo erectus
and later species from earlier hominins.
The argument is this. Cooking increases
the caloric yield of food dramatically,
allowing the same amount of food to
deliver significantly more usable
energy. This meant that early humans
could spend less time eating and less
energy on digestion. And when the body
no longer needs to devote enormous
resources to a massive digestive system,
those resources become available for
other things. Specifically, the brain.
The human brain is metabolically
expensive in a way that is genuinely
extreme. It consumes roughly 20% of the
body's total energy at rest. A wildly
disproportionate share for an organ that
represents only about 2% of body mass.
Sustaining a brain this large requires
either a very high-calorie diet or a
reduced investment in other
energetically expensive body systems.
The human gut is, compared to other
great apes, significantly smaller. Our
teeth are smaller. Our jaw muscles are
smaller. We have a reduced digestive
tract overall. These are the anatomical
signatures of a species that outsourced
part of its digestion to an external
process, cooking, and redirected the
freed energy toward brain development.
This is not a small claim.
It is a claim that fire literally and
directly made us smarter. That the
cognitive capacity you are using right
now to follow this argument exists
partly because some ancestor of yours
discovered that meat goes further and
tastes better when you put it near
flames for a while. The timing of Homo
erectus's emergence and the earliest
evidence of controlled fire use aligns
suggestively with this hypothesis. Homo
erectus had a significantly larger brain
than earlier hominins, a significantly
